title: Measurement Error

findings.finding: The garden question requires students to bound a calculated area before teaching how to combine measurement bounds.
findings.breakdown: Students must choose the lower bound of both dimensions before multiplying. The preceding examples bound only individual measurements, leaving a plausible incorrect approach of subtracting 0.5 from the recorded area of 15 m².
findings.checked: All supplied teaching before p5-e was checked. p4-limits-formulas-method and both p4 examples explain bounds of individual measurements; p5-a–d practise those bounds. None explains bounds of a product. p9-q14 later supplies a dimension-to-area scaffold, but cannot prepare students for p5-e.
findings.assumptions: Students know the rectangle area formula. Combining measurement bounds to bound an area is new within this booklet. Calculator availability does not affect the finding.

repair.proposal: Before p5-e add: “For a rectangle with positive dimensions, the smallest possible area uses the lower bound of each dimension. Find both lower bounds, then multiply them.”

findings.doneWhen: Before p5-e, students are explicitly taught to bound both dimensions before calculating the lower area bound.

findings.finding: Compare the unequal area changes produced by equal changes in the measured side.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the calculated area bounds to the recorded area and exposes why area uncertainty is not symmetric about that area.
findings.checked: p9-q14 supplies side bounds of 14.5 cm and 15.5 cm and corresponding area bounds of 210.25 cm² and 240.25 cm². The recorded area is 225 cm²; the differences are 14.75 cm² and 15.25 cm². Only area calculation and subtraction are required.
findings.assumptions: Students use their answers to p9-q14-b and p9-q14-d.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts after p9-q14-e: (f) “What area is calculated using the recorded side length of 15 cm?” Answer: 225 cm². (g) “How far below 225 cm² is the lower area bound?” Answer: 14.75 cm². (h) “How far above 225 cm² is the upper area bound?” Answer: 15.25 cm².

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts use the existing square and correctly compare both area bounds with 225 cm².

findings.finding: Hold measured magnitude constant while varying recorded precision.
findings.breakdown: The run exposes that reducing precision by a factor of ten reduces the unrounded percentage error by the same factor when measured magnitude stays constant.
findings.checked: The complete supplied practice contains no equivalent run. Using p10-definition, the percentage errors for 24 m, 24.0 m and 24.00 m are approximately 2.083%, 0.208% and 0.021%. For 37.2 m the percentage error is approximately 0.134%. Trailing zeros indicate precision under p3-precision and p3-identify.
findings.assumptions: A calculator is available, consistent with the existing percentage-error calculations to three decimal places.

repair.proposal: Retain the existing Harbour Bridge task as part (a), then append further parts under its instruction to calculate percentage error to three decimal places. Add only this instruction: “Predict how the percentage error will change before calculating.” (b) 24 m; answer: 2.083%. (c) 24.0 m; answer: 0.208%. (d) 24.00 m; answer: 0.021%. (e) 37.2 m; answer: 0.134%. In (b)–(d), magnitude and units stay constant while precision varies; (e) is the unpatterned follow-up.

findings.doneWhen: The three comparison measurements and one unpatterned measurement follow p12-q6, with only the single prediction instruction added.

findings.finding: Double the measured mass while retaining the same precision.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up exposes that unchanged absolute error gives half the percentage error when measured mass doubles.
findings.checked: Both 49.6 kg and 99.2 kg have precision 0.1 kg and absolute error 0.05 kg. Their unrounded percentage errors are approximately 0.100806% and 0.050403%, respectively. The second is exactly half the first before rounding. All required methods appear in p10-definition and its examples.
findings.assumptions: A calculator is available, consistent with the topic's existing decimal calculations.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts to p11-q2: (c) “Another dishwasher is measured as 99.2 kg. Find its percentage error to three decimal places.” Answer: 0.050%. (d) “Before rounding, how does this percentage error compare with that for 49.6 kg? Explain why.” Answer: It is half as large because the absolute error remains 0.05 kg while the measured mass doubles.

findings.doneWhen: The optional comparison explicitly concerns unrounded percentage errors, avoiding distortion from the original part's two-decimal-place answer.
